summary:
The input is sorted, so the biggest square comes from one of the two ends (the most negative or the most
positive value). Compare the ends' absolute values, write the larger square into the last free slot of the
output, and move that pointer inward. O(n).

question.md:
`values` is sorted (with negatives); return all squares in increasing order, in **O(n)**.

- **Negatives flip order** when squared: −7 squares to 49, bigger than 6².
- **Up to 10⁵ values**, |value| ≤ 10⁴ (squares fit in 32 bits).

think.md:
`[-7, -3, -1, 2, 4, 6]` squares to `[49, 9, 1, 4, 16, 36]`; sorted: `[1, 4, 9, 16, 36, 49]`.

The squares are smallest near zero and grow toward **both** ends. So the largest remaining square is always at
the left end or the right end. Taking the larger of the two each time produces the squares from largest to
smallest: fill the output from the back.

idea.md: Square every value and sort the result.

steps.text: Squares: [49, 9, 1, 4, 16, 36]. The negatives' squares are out of order.

limits.md: Misses the O(n) requirement and ignores that the input is sorted: the squares are two sorted runs (negatives reversed, then non-negatives) that only need merging.

approaches.title: Two pointers, fill from the back

idea.md: `i = 0`, `j = n − 1`. For `k` from `n − 1` down to 0: put the larger of `values[i]²` and `values[j]²` at `out[k]` and move that pointer inward.

build: Fill from the back with the larger square.

lines.text: The output and pointers at both ends.
Fill from the largest slot down.
The larger absolute value at either end gives the largest remaining square.

steps.text: |-7| > |6|: write 49 at position 5, move i right.
|6| ≥ |-3|: write 36 at position 4, move j left.
|4| ≥ |-3|: write 16 at position 3, move j left.
|-3| > |2|: write 9 at position 2, move i right.
|2| ≥ |-1|: write 4 at position 1, move j left.
|-1| ≥ |-1|: write 1 at position 0, move j left.

walk.title: The largest square is at one of the two ends. Fill the output from the back, taking the end with the bigger absolute value.

takeaways.md:
- **Sorted input with negatives:** the extremes are at both ends; two pointers merge them.
- Filling the output from the back avoids having to find the smallest square first.
- It's a merge of two sorted runs in disguise.
